passage:
Every human body keeps time. Deep in the brain sits a small cluster of cells that acts as an internal clock, telling us when to feel alert and when to feel tired. This rhythm repeats roughly every twenty-four hours, and it is set mainly by light. When morning light reaches the eye, the clock resets; when darkness falls, the body begins producing a hormone called melatonin, which prepares it for sleep.

Night-shift workers live in conflict with this system. Nurses, factory staff, pilots and security guards are awake when their bodies expect rest, and they try to sleep when daylight is telling the clock to wake up. The result is not simply tiredness. Studies have linked long-term night work with digestive complaints, heart problems and a higher risk of certain illnesses.

The damage is not evenly spread. People differ in how easily they adjust, and a minority cope well for years. Age matters as well: workers over forty generally find night shifts harder than younger colleagues do.

Some employers have begun to take the problem seriously. Rotating shifts forward — morning, then afternoon, then night — suits the body better than rotating them backwards. Bright lighting in the workplace during the shift, and dark curtains at home afterwards, can shift the clock a little. Short naps before a shift begins also help.

None of these measures removes the conflict entirely. The internal clock cannot be switched off, only nudged. For as long as hospitals, power stations and airports run through the night, somebody will be awake when their body would rather not be.
